summary.one_line: A fast-growing, debt-funded forklift and warehouse-equipment rental business from Delhi raising ₹120.10 crore, all of it fresh capital, mostly to buy more fleet. The growth is real, but there is no visible moat, free cash flow is negative, and the governance flags are serious enough to watch the stock after listing rather than apply now.
bull_points: The issue is 100% fresh (49.02 lakh shares, ₹120.10 crore) with no offer for sale, so all the money goes into the company and promoters sell nothing (S1, S2).

Revenue from operations grew from ₹130.12 crore in FY24 to ₹211.36 crore in FY26 (about 27% CAGR). PAT grew from ₹18.05 crore to ₹29.16 crore over the same period, with EBITDA margins steady at about 29-31% (S9, S1).

The customer base is spread out. The top five customers were only 15.12% of FY26 revenue from operations, down from 20.74% in FY24, across automotive, tyres, beverages, glass, paper and logistics (S12, S1).
About ₹98.13 crore of the proceeds goes to income-generating fleet: MHE ₹65.02 crore, aerial work platforms ₹14.58 crore and batteries ₹18.52 crore (S12, S1).
Operating cash flow covers reported profit: FY26 operating cash flow was ₹48.68 crore against PAT of ₹29.16 crore (S12, S18).
bear_points: There is no real moat. Forklift rental is a capital-and-manpower business, and OEMs such as Godrej and Jungheinrich offer rentals themselves (S24, S23).
Borrowings rose from ₹93.12 crore (FY24) to ₹164.72 crore (June 2026), and none of the issue money goes to repaying debt (S1, S4).
Free cash flow is deeply negative. FY26 investing outflow of ₹91.39 crore was almost double operating cash flow, and borrowing filled the gap (S18, S12).

Governance flags: the company bought MHE from a promoter-group entity without a formal purchase agreement and without generating e-way bills. The RHP also discloses delayed or erroneous Companies Act filings and promoter interests in similar businesses (S14, S16, S12).
Returns are falling as the fleet grows. RoCE was 24.11% in FY24, 23.85% in FY25 and 19.06% in FY26 (S9).
watch_points: Whether the new fleet earns its keep: RoCE and EBITDA margin in the first two half-years after listing, against 19.06% RoCE and a 30.76% EBITDA margin in FY26 (S9).
Any GST or regulatory consequence of the undocumented promoter-group equipment purchases (S14, S15).
Status of the material civil case reported at ₹16.00 crore against the company and promoters. Only one secondary source reports it (S12).
Lock-in expiry dates: anchor shares (50% after 30 days, the rest after 90 days) and promoters' shares beyond their minimum contribution (S1, S25).
Final subscription mix. QIB bids were nil on the morning of day 1 (S13).

reasoning: The use of money is sound but adds nothing new. About ₹98 crore buys more forklifts, aerial work platforms and batteries, which is just more of the existing business. No debt is repaid, so the ₹164.72 crore loan book stays on the balance sheet, and the issue mainly lets the company keep growing its fleet without borrowing more (S12, S1, S4).

Growth is real, but it is bought with capital and earns falling returns. Revenue grew about 27% a year from FY24 to FY26 at steady 29-31% EBITDA margins. Over the same period RoCE fell from 24.11% to 19.06%, and FY26 capex of ₹91.39 crore was almost double operating cash flow (S9, S18). Nothing has yet shown that this keeps working as the fleet doubles.

There is no moat to protect returns. The company is a large independent renter (2,679 units, 500+ sites, 24-25 states) with low customer concentration. It sources new equipment from third parties such as Hangcha and competes with OEM-backed rental offerings. Scale and service are its only edges, and both can be copied (S9, S12, S6, S23, S24).

Governance is the deciding factor against applying now. The RHP-derived disclosures cite undocumented equipment purchases from a promoter-group entity with no e-way bills, delayed or erroneous statutory filings, promoter interests in similar businesses, promoters as the only managers, and a reported ₹16 crore material civil case. The issue also needed a refiled DRHP (S14, S16, S12, S3).

Track rather than avoid, because the underlying business is real and cash-generative at the operating level. A few half-years of listed disclosure would show whether utilisation, margins and RoCE hold up after the fleet expansion and whether the related-party issues are cleaned up (S12, S9).

blocks.text: Watrana Rentals was incorporated in Delhi on 19 November 2019 as Watrana Rentals Private Limited and became a public company in December 2024 (S19, S4). Its main business is renting material handling equipment (MHE) to factories and warehouses. The fleet covers battery, diesel and gas forklifts, electric stackers, reach trucks, pallet trucks, order pickers, towing trucks and attachments such as paper-roll clamps, bale clamps and side shifters. It has recently added aerial work platforms (AWPs) (S1, S6, S9).

The company has three revenue lines: (1) rental of MHE and AWPs, (2) trading in new and used MHE, and (3) trading in batteries for MHE, sold to both rental and trading customers (S1, S9). Rental is most of the business, at 87.66% of FY26 revenue from operations (S9). The remaining ~12% is equipment and battery trading. The sources we could read do not split that remainder further.

Pricing works as an outsourcing contract. Customers rent equipment instead of buying it, and contracts can include operators, maintenance, technicians and replacement units (S6, S9). This explains why the company has a very large workforce for its size: about 3,883 personnel at 30 June 2026 (S1, S9). Much of that workforce is likely operators deployed at customer sites, so the business is both capital-heavy and manpower-heavy.

Think of this as an equipment-plus-operator outsourcing business, not a manufacturer. Profit depends on buying forklifts cheaply, keeping them rented (utilisation), and financing them more cheaply than they earn.

The fleet has grown quickly. Secondary summaries of the 2025 DRHP put the operational fleet at about 1,441 MHE units at 30 April 2025, with about 304 rental sites and 3,122 people (S5, S4). By 31 March 2026 the fleet was 2,549 units across more than 630 rental/customer sites in 25 states (S12). At 30 June 2026 the company owned 2,646 MHE and 33 AWP units, and rented a further 5 MHE and 2 AWP units from third parties (S1, S17). One summary gives 515 sites in 24 states at June 2026 (S9), which differs from the March 2026 site count. The definitions may differ, and we could not check this against the RHP.

blocks.caption: Operating scale over time (from secondary summaries of the DRHP/RHP)

blocks.text: The registered office is in Derawal Nagar, Delhi. The operating base (office and works) is at the UPSIDC Industrial Area, Kasna, Greater Noida, according to the company's own letterhead on its anchor-allocation filing (S7). The company holds ISO 9001:2015, ISO 45001:2018 and ISO 14001:2015 certifications (S5, S12). These are standard quality, safety and environment certifications, not barriers to entry.

Customers come from automotive, tyres, food and beverages, glass, paper, chemicals, general manufacturing, and logistics and warehousing (S1, S12, S9). Concentration is low for an SME. The top five customers contributed ₹31.68 crore, or 15.12% of FY26 revenue from operations, down from 20.74% in FY24 (S12). The RHP still lists customer concentration as a risk, and it notes that customers can end contracts without cause on short notice (S14, S6). This matters more than the concentration figure itself: rental revenue is contractual but not locked in.

The supply side is the more concentrated part. The company sells and deploys equipment from third-party brands, including Toyota, Hangcha and Dingli (S9). New MHE for trading is sourced from Zhejiang Hangcha Imp & Exp Co. Ltd., a Chinese OEM (S6, S12). The company also relies on third parties for equipment, AWP and battery supply, and for maintenance and servicing of its fleet (S12, S16). It has also bought MHE from a promoter-group entity (S14), covered under governance.

items: Buy (or rent in) equipment, mostly imported or OEM-sourced, largely financed with secured bank and NBFC debt (S12, S14).
Deploy it at customer sites with optional operators, technicians and maintenance on a rental contract (S6, S9).
Earn monthly rental. Trade surplus or used units and batteries on the side (S1).
Margin drivers are utilisation, rental rates, maintenance and battery costs, depreciation and interest (S2, S9).

blocks.text: We could not open the RHP's business section directly. Top-10 customer and supplier percentages, the rental-rate structure and fleet utilisation were not available in any source we could read, so they are not stated here.

We found no reliable India-specific figure for the forklift rental market. IMARC sizes the whole India forklift market (sales, not just rental) at USD 8.2 billion in 2025 and USD 9.4 billion in 2026, forecasting USD 23.6 billion by 2034, a 12.16% CAGR for 2026-2034. It lists rental-market expansion among the growth drivers but gives no rental-only figure (S21). Other research houses' estimates for the same market differ by more than double, so treat any single market-size number with caution.

The qualitative case for rental is consistent across sources. ACE's forklift CEO said in 2021 that India's MHE rental market had been growing and that companies were outsourcing material handling to rental firms to save manpower and capital (S22). Jungheinrich India and Godrej said the same year that customers were shifting from purchase to rental to save capex (S23, S24). Warehousing, logistics and manufacturing growth are the demand drivers the IPO summaries cite (S10, S9).

The industry evidence here is directional and partly dated (2021 trade-press interviews). It supports the idea that rental demand is growing. It does not support a specific market size or market-share claim for Watrana.

The competition is real and well-resourced. Large forklift OEMs rent directly: Jungheinrich India offers long- and short-term rental of new and used equipment (S23), and Godrej Material Handling offers rental fleets with telematics, backed by 90+ customer touchpoints (S24). The company's own risk factors describe competition from organised operators, OEM-backed platforms, regional players and smaller providers, which may pressure rates and margins (S9). We found no named, listed pure-play rental competitor in the sources we could read.

items: No import-substitution story. The company is a buyer of OEM equipment, including from China (S6, S12).
No market-share claim or 'only Indian player' claim appeared in any summary of the offer document we could read.
No regulatory licence acts as a barrier to entry. ISO certifications are standard (S5).

Its real advantages are scale and network: a 2,679-unit fleet, 500+ sites, a trained operator workforce and a diversified customer base (S1, S9, S12). These help win multi-site contracts but can be copied by anyone with capital.

blocks.text: Plain answer: no genuine moat. This is a well-run, scale-driven rental business in a commoditised segment where OEMs compete directly. Returns will depend on execution (utilisation and cost of capital), not on structural protection.

blocks.caption: Restated financials, ₹ crore (FY = year to 31 March; Q1 FY27 = three months to 30 June 2026, not annualised)

blocks.text: Revenue-from-operations and margin figures are from S9, which reports them in ₹ million; we converted to crore. Total income, EBITDA and PAT are from S1, S5 and S2, and they match across all three. Revenue grew 37.9% in FY25 and 17.8% in FY26. PAT grew 35.3% and 19.4%, about 27% a year compounded over two years (our calculation from S1). Growth halved in FY26 even though FY26 capex was roughly double FY25's. The extra fleet bought in FY26 had not yet shown up in a full year of revenue, so the question is whether FY27 revenue catches up.

Going further back, the 2025 DRHP showed revenue of ₹47.30 crore and PAT of ₹3.94 crore in FY22, and ₹86.12 crore and ₹8.52 crore in FY23. PAT margin rose from 8.32% in FY22 to 13.87% in FY24 (S4). Margins rose in FY22-FY24 and have stayed in a narrow 13.6-14.4% PAT band since. That suggests the business has reached a stable unit economics level rather than one that is still improving.

RoCE fell from 24.11% to 19.06% over FY24-FY26 (S9). The June 2026 quarter's 4.87% annualises to roughly 19.5%, so it is flat. Each new rupee of fleet is earning less than the old fleet did. That is the main financial question for a capital-heavy rental model.

subsections.title: Balance sheet, leverage and cash flow

blocks.caption: Balance sheet and cash flow, ₹ crore

blocks.text: Balance sheet figures are from S1 and S5. Cash flows are from S18, converted from ₹ lakh. One aggregator gives FY24 operating cash flow as ₹31.01 crore rather than ₹32.25 crore (S6), which is a minor difference. Net worth grew each year by exactly that year's PAT (₹24.43 crore in FY25, ₹29.16 crore in FY26; our check from S1), so no outside equity came in and no dividends went out. All growth has been funded by retained profit plus debt.

Earnings quality is fine: operating cash flow was 1.4-1.8x PAT in every year (S18, S1). That is normal for a rental business with large depreciation. Free cash flow is negative, however. FY26 operating cash flow of ₹48.68 crore against investing outflow of ₹91.39 crore leaves a gap of about ₹42.7 crore, which new borrowing filled (S18, S12). Leverage fell from 2.9x to about 1.8x of net worth because profits were retained. One aggregator reports a 2.91 debt/equity figure as at March 2026 (S1, S11), but that does not fit its own borrowing and net-worth numbers, which give about 1.9x. It appears to be the FY24 ratio carried forward.

Contingent liabilities were ₹2.77 crore at December 2024, according to the 2025 DRHP summary (S4). We could not find the current figure. Borrowings are secured on the fleet and carry restrictive covenants, so a default could lead lenders to enforce against the charged equipment (S14, S16).

subsections.title: Does the trend support the growth story?

blocks.text: Partly. Revenue, EBITDA and PAT have all compounded at roughly 27% a year over FY24-FY26 on steady margins (S1, S9). The June 2026 quarter's EBITDA margin of 33.91% was the best in the series (S1). That is a solid record for a company only six and a half years old. But the 2025 DRHP planned ₹99.67 crore of equipment purchases across FY26 and FY27 from IPO money (S4, S3). When that IPO did not happen in 2025, the company did much of the FY26 expansion with debt instead (S18, S1). The new IPO will now fund a further round of fleet growth on top of that.

items: Supportive: steady margins, operating cash flow above PAT, falling customer concentration (S9, S18, S12).
Not supportive: FY26 revenue growth slowed to ~18% despite a much larger capex year, and RoCE is trending down (S1, S9).
Unknown: fleet utilisation and rental yield per unit. Neither appears in any source we could read.

blocks.text: Our rough calculation, not from the RHP: with about ₹110 crore of net issue money and no debt repayment, borrowings/net worth would fall to roughly 0.8x after the issue if debt stayed flat. The capital structure becomes comfortable, but the company has not committed to cutting debt.

sections.title: Issue details and objects of the issue

blocks.caption: Key terms
rows: 49,02,000 shares, ~₹120.10 crore at the top of the band (S1)
100% fresh issue, nil offer for sale (S1, S2)
600 shares; individuals must bid 2 lots (1,200 shares) = ₹2,94,000 (S1)
Anchor 18 Nov; open 19 Nov; close 23 Nov; allotment 25 Nov; listing 27 Nov 2026 (S1)

blocks.text: Some broker pages show a 1,200-share lot, and one shows an OFS component (S14, S15). The more detailed trackers and the review say the lot is 600 shares with a two-lot minimum for individuals, and that the issue is wholly fresh (S1, S2, S8). We go with the majority. Retail applicants should check the RHP or their broker before bidding.
No promoter is selling. All ₹120.10 crore goes to the company, before issue expenses. Promoter ownership falls from 100% to about 70% (S1, S5).

The capex split is from S12. The ₹98.13 crore total is from S1 and S2. One broker note gives general corporate purposes as ₹27 crore but says itself that this does not reconcile with the issue size (S10), so we treat the GCP figure as unconfirmed. No proceeds go to repaying debt. This was also true of the 2025 DRHP, which earmarked ₹99.67 crore for MHE and batteries (₹34.34 crore in FY26 and ₹65.34 crore in FY27) and left GCP blank (S4, S3).

From an investor's point of view, this is growth capital in the strictest sense. The money buys revenue-earning assets in the company's existing business, and nothing goes out to promoters or old investors. The other side is that it is pure execution risk. Each new forklift or AWP only adds value if it is rented out at good utilisation, and the declining RoCE trend shows that has become harder as the fleet grew (S9). AWPs are a relatively new product line for the company (S9), so the ₹14.58 crore AWP spend carries extra risk of being a new line the company has not yet proven.

Equipment purchases are where the governance questions come in. The company has previously bought MHE from a promoter-group entity without a formal agreement (S14). Investors should check the RHP to see whether any of the ₹98 crore can go to related-party vendors.

The promoters are Sanjeev Kumar Watrana (Managing Director, 51), Rajeev Kumar Watrana (Whole-Time Director, 48) and Neha Watrana (S6, S1). The two brothers each have more than 15 years in the MHE industry (S9). The 2025 DRHP showed Sanjeev and Rajeev holding 50,04,975 shares each, about 49.99% apiece (S4). After the issue the promoter group will own about 70% (S1, S5). One aggregator shows 73.5% (S11) and another 35% (S19). The 70% figure fits the share counts, since 1,14,38,500 pre-issue shares out of 1,63,40,500 post-issue is exactly 70%.

Their track record goes back before this company. A profile of Rajeev Watrana links to Watrana Traction Pvt. Ltd., described there as a material-handling manufacturer, importer and distributor formed in 2003. It distributes the NICHIYU and SUN-TWS brands and also ran a forklift rental service (S20). That gives the family real industry experience. It also suggests the promoters have related businesses in the same field. The RHP summaries confirm promoters have interests in group entities with similar businesses, which can create conflicts of interest (S12, S16). The company filed its anchor letter on a letterhead using a forkliftspares.com e-mail address (S7). This is a small sign that the family's businesses are closely intertwined.

The bench is thin. One summary says the company has two executive directors and that the promoters remain its only managers (S12). There is no evidence in the sources we could read of an independent CFO or operations head with a separate track record. For a company with 3,800+ staff, 500+ sites and ₹165 crore of debt, the business depends heavily on two people.

This is not a routine RPT section. Several independent summaries of the RHP's risk factors report that the company bought MHE from a promoter-group entity without a formal purchase agreement, and that no e-way bills were generated for these transactions. The company itself flags possible GST and regulatory non-compliance as a result (S14, S15, S16). For a business that exists to buy and deploy equipment, buying fleet from the promoters' own company without paperwork is a real red flag. It raises questions about transfer pricing as well as tax compliance.

items: Undocumented MHE purchases from a promoter-group entity, with no e-way bills and possible GST exposure (S14, S15).
Promoters have interests in entities with similar or overlapping businesses (MHE rental and battery trading) (S12, S16).
Past delays, omissions or errors in statutory filings under the Companies Act, 2013 (S12, S16).
One material civil case involving ₹16.00 crore against the company and its promoters (S12). Only one secondary source reports this and we could not verify its nature.
The IPO took a second attempt: a DRHP dated 30 June 2025, then a refiled DRHP in August 2026 (S4, S3). No source gives the reason.

blocks.text: We could not read the full RPT table (amounts of purchases, rent, loans and remuneration with named entities) because the RHP itself could not be fetched. Given the flags above, a prospective investor should read the RHP's 'Related Party Transactions' and 'Outstanding Litigation' chapters before applying.

items: Leverage and refinancing: ₹164.72 crore of secured borrowings at June 2026 with restrictive covenants. Lenders can enforce against the charged fleet on default, and none of the IPO money repays debt (S1, S14, S16).
Utilisation and capital intensity: idle equipment still costs depreciation, interest, insurance, storage and maintenance. RoCE has already slipped from 24.11% to 19.06% (S9, S2).
Governance and related parties: undocumented equipment purchases from a promoter-group entity with possible GST exposure, plus promoter interests in similar businesses (S14, S16, S12).
Litigation and compliance: a reported ₹16 crore material civil case and a history of delayed or erroneous Companies Act filings (S12).

Supplier and service dependence: equipment, AWPs and batteries come from third parties, including a Chinese OEM, and fleet maintenance is partly outsourced. Supply disruption, currency or cost changes could hurt expansion (S12, S6, S9).
Cyclical end-markets and short contracts: demand depends on automotive, manufacturing, warehousing and logistics activity, and customers can end contracts at short notice (S9, S6).
Key-person risk: the promoters are effectively the whole management team (S12).

blocks.text: We left out the boilerplate risks (general market risk, no prior market for the shares, book-built price discovery) that every prospectus repeats (S6). The seven above are the ones that could actually lower earnings or the investor's claim on them. The first three would on their own justify waiting for post-listing evidence.
The ₹16 crore litigation figure comes from a single aggregator (S12). We did not see the RHP's litigation chapter. Treat it as a pointer to check, not a confirmed fact.

SME shares trade in fixed lots through a market maker, so liquidity after listing can be thin and getting out may be hard (S2, S12). Here the minimum application is ₹2.94 lakh (S1), so a retail investor puts a large single sum into one illiquid stock.

Anchor investors hold 13,86,000 shares (28.27% of the issue). Half are locked in until 25 December 2026 (30 days) and the rest until 23 February 2027 (90 days) (S1). Those dates are possible supply-overhang points. For promoters, SEBI's December 2024 SME framework locks the minimum promoter contribution for three years. Holdings above that minimum are released 50% after one year and 50% after two years (S25). SEBI's October 2026 consultation proposes cutting the excess lock-in to a single year (S26). We could not confirm from the RHP which terms apply to this issue, so this is the general rule, not a verified issue-specific term.

Unexplained share-count change: share capital implied by the restated accounts was about ₹10.01 crore at June 2026, about 1.0 crore shares (S1). The pre-issue count is 1,14,38,500 shares (S1). No source we read explains the roughly 14.4 lakh additional shares, so check the RHP's capital-structure chapter.

The only concrete forward plan we found is the objects of the issue itself: ₹65.02 crore of MHE, ₹14.58 crore of AWPs and ₹18.52 crore of batteries to be bought with the proceeds (S12). The 2025 DRHP phased a similar plan across FY26 and FY27 (S4). The company's stated strategy, as summarised from the offer document, is to keep growing a large, diversified fleet across more sites, build out the newer AWP line, and benefit from manufacturing, warehousing, logistics and e-commerce demand along with customers' preference for renting over buying (S9).

We found no investor call, management interview or numeric guidance (revenue targets, fleet targets, utilisation goals or debt-reduction targets) in any source we could open. The RHP's management discussion section could not be read directly. The honest outlook is therefore 'more of the same, faster': fleet growth funded by the IPO. Whether that brings the earnings growth back above FY26's ~18% is not something management has publicly committed to.

The June 2026 quarter is the latest evidence: revenue ₹53.47 crore, PAT ₹7.68 crore and a 33.91% EBITDA margin (S9, S1). That is on track for modest growth over FY26 if sustained, but one quarter is not a trend.

items: Positive: RoCE stabilises at or above ~20% as IPO-funded fleet is deployed, and revenue growth picks back up toward the FY25 pace (S9, S1).
Positive: clear disclosure that related-party equipment purchases have ended or are formally documented at arm's length, and that the GST exposure is settled (S14).
Negative: any new borrowing on top of the IPO money, a lender covenant issue, or adverse developments in the reported ₹16 crore case (S12, S16).
Negative: EBITDA margins slipping below the 29-31% band as competition from OEM rental offerings intensifies (S9, S23, S24).

blocks.text: As a listed SME the company will publish half-yearly results. Two such reports, covering FY27 and the first half of FY28, would answer most of these questions without the investor having to commit ₹2.94 lakh up front (S1).

subsections.title: Anchors, day-1 bids and grey market

blocks.text: On 18 November 2026 the company allotted 13,86,000 shares to eight anchor investors at ₹245, raising ₹33.96 crore (S7). The largest were Old Bridge Flexi Cap Fund (4,08,600 shares, 29.48% of the anchor book, the only domestic mutual fund), Massachusetts Institute of Technology (3,27,600 shares, 23.64%) and SageOne Small and Micro Opportunity Fund (2,77,800 shares, 20.04%). The others were BTH Classic Growth Fund, Aarth AIF Growth Fund, 238 Plan Associates LLC, Steptrade Revolution Fund and Ekamya Pragati Scheme I (S7). Anchor lock-in is 50% for 30 days and 50% for 90 days (S1).

blocks.caption: Day-1 subscription snapshots, 19 Nov 2026 (partial and changing; times IST)

blocks.text: These are early-morning snapshots on the first of four bidding days, with 1,420 applications at the 10:55 reading (S13). They say almost nothing about final demand. QIB bids usually arrive on the last day. The grey market premium was reported at ₹62 (about 25%) on 19 November, up from ₹16 on 13 November, with a jump on anchor day (S5, S6). This figure is unofficial and unregulated, and other sources earlier reported different levels (S2). It is not part of our investment case.
Anchor names like MIT and Old Bridge make a good headline, but anchors can exit half their stake after 30 days (S1). Their participation does not resolve the governance and RoCE questions above.

method: Researched on 2026-11-19, the day the issue opened. MATERIAL GAP: we did not read the RHP or DRHP directly. The RHP is on NSE as RHP_WATRANA.zip and the original DRHP at nsearchives.nseindia.com (Registration_30062025193837_DRHPWRL.pdf); both timed out on every fetch attempt, and direct download tools were not available. The analysis therefore rests on secondary summaries of the offer document, cross-checked against each other. Restated FY24-FY26 and Q1 FY27 P&L and balance-sheet figures matched across at least four independent aggregators (S1, S2, S5, S8, S11, S12, S17). Revenue-from-operations, margins and RoCE come from Angel One (S9). Cash flows come from Finowings (S18) and IPOGuru (S12). Customer concentration, the capex split of the objects, litigation (₹16 crore) and the single-geography/delayed-filing risks come mainly from IPOGuru (S12). The related-party purchase flag is confirmed by three broker pages (S14, S15, S16). The ₹16 crore litigation and the general-corporate-purposes amount each rest on one source and are flagged as unverified. The anchor allocation was read from the company's own exchange filing (S7). Not available from any source we could read: the full RPT table with amounts, top-10 customer and supplier shares, fleet utilisation, issue-specific promoter lock-in terms, the reason for the 2025-to-2026 DRHP refiling, and the source of the ~14.4 lakh-share increase between June 2026 and the pre-issue count. Aggregator conflicts were resolved toward the majority figure and noted in the text: lot size 600 vs 1,200, fresh-only vs an OFS shown by one site, post-issue promoter holding 70% vs 73.5%/35%, and debt/equity 2.91 vs ~1.9 computed. Industry sizing is for the whole India forklift market (IMARC), not rental-only, and trade-press competitor evidence dates from 2021. Valuation was deliberately excluded per the brief, and P/E or market-cap figures shown by sources were ignored. GMP and subscription are reported only as labelled context, not as inputs to the verdict.
